questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.syllabus_ref: 3.5 Profitability and liquidity ratio analysis (gross, operating and net profit margins, ROCE, current ratio, acid test); 3.4 Final accounts
questions.subtopic: 3.5 Two transactions that move the liquidity ratios in opposite directions, and the cancellation inside the acid test

stimulus.title: Marlowe Supplies: extract from the final accounts for the year ended 31 March
stimulus.body:
The income statement for the year shows revenue of $\pounds 480{,}000$ and cost of goods sold of $\pounds 300{,}000$. Operating expenses were $\pounds 120{,}000$, interest payable was $\pounds 12{,}000$ and tax was $\pounds 9{,}600$.

The statement of financial position at the year end is summarised below. All figures are in pounds, and there are no other current assets and no other current liabilities.

table.caption: Statement of financial position at 31 March.

questions.challenge_mechanism: A ratio is not a quantity, and reasoning about it by reasoning about the numbers inside it gives the wrong direction of change. Whether a transaction that reduces both current assets and current liabilities raises or lowers the current ratio depends on whether the ratio was above or below one, which is a property of the ratio rather than of the transaction. The acid test adds a second trap: buying inventory on credit raises current assets and current liabilities by the same amount, so the equal-amounts rule applies to the current ratio, but the acid test subtracts inventory out of the numerator, so the addition and the subtraction cancel and the numerator does not move at all.
questions.question: Marlowe Supplies is a single-product wholesaler. The figures above are taken from its final accounts for the year just ended. Before those figures are finalised the business is considering two transactions: paying a supplier $\pounds 10{,}000$ in cash, and then buying $\pounds 30{,}000$ of inventory on credit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross profit margin, the operating profit margin and the net profit margin.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the return on capital employed, stating which figure you have used as the numerator and which as the denominator.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the current ratio and the acid test ratio at the position shown.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The business pays a supplier $\pounds 10{,}000$ in cash. Show that both the current ratio and the acid test ratio rise, and explain why a payment that reduces current assets and current liabilities by the same amount improves both ratios.

parts.label: e
parts.text: The business then buys $\pounds 30{,}000$ of inventory on credit. Show that the acid test ratio falls to 0.81, and evaluate whether the two transactions together leave Marlowe Supplies in a stronger or a weaker liquidity position than it began in.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Gross profit is revenue less cost of goods sold, so (M1)

$$\pounds 480{,}000 - \pounds 300{,}000 = \pounds 180{,}000 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{180{,}000}{480{,}000} = 37.5\% \tag{A1}$$

Operating profit deducts the operating expenses: $\pounds 180{,}000 - \pounds 120{,}000 = \pounds 60{,}000$, so the operating profit margin is $60{,}000/480{,}000 = 12.5\%$ (A1).

Net profit also deducts interest and tax: $\pounds 60{,}000 - \pounds 12{,}000 - \pounds 9{,}600 = \pounds 38{,}400$, so the net profit margin is $38{,}400/480{,}000 = 8.0\%$ (A1).

The three margins fall by design: each one deducts a further layer of cost, so the sequence $37.5\%$, $12.5\%$, $8.0\%$ is a description of where the revenue goes. The largest single deduction is the $\pounds 120{,}000$ of operating expenses, which takes 25 percentage points of revenue and is the reason the gross margin is three times the operating margin.

**(b)** Capital employed is the long-term money in the business, which here is equity plus non-current liabilities (M1):

$$\pounds 200{,}000 + \pounds 100{,}000 = \pounds 300{,}000$$

Return on capital employed is operating profit divided by capital employed (M1):

$$\frac{60{,}000}{300{,}000} = 20.0\% \tag{A1}$$

The numerator must be operating profit, not net profit. Using net profit would give $38{,}400/300{,}000 = 12.8\%$, which understates the return on the assets because it charges the capital employed with interest that has already been deducted in arriving at net profit. Using equity alone as the denominator would give $60{,}000/200{,}000 = 30.0\%$, which overstates it by leaving the non-current liabilities out of the capital they helped to fund.

**(c)** Current assets are inventory, receivables and cash (M1):

$$\pounds 45{,}000 + \pounds 60{,}000 + \pounds 15{,}000 = \pounds 120{,}000$$

The current ratio is current assets over current liabilities (A1):

$$\frac{120{,}000}{60{,}000} = 2.00$$

The acid test removes inventory from the numerator, because inventory is the current asset least likely to convert to cash at its book value (A1):

$$\frac{120{,}000 - 45{,}000}{60{,}000} = \frac{75{,}000}{60{,}000} = 1.25$$

**(d)** Paying $\pounds 10{,}000$ in cash reduces cash to $\pounds 5{,}000$, so current assets become $\pounds 110{,}000$ and current liabilities become $\pounds 50{,}000$ (M1).

$$\text{current ratio} = \frac{110{,}000}{50{,}000} = 2.20 \qquad \text{acid test} = \frac{110{,}000 - 45{,}000}{50{,}000} = \frac{65{,}000}{50{,}000} = 1.30 \tag{A1}$$

Both ratios rise, from 2.00 to 2.20 and from 1.25 to 1.30, even though the business is now smaller by $\pounds 10{,}000$ of cash (A1).

The reason is that the same amount leaves the top and the bottom of the fraction. Writing the current ratio as $a/b$ with $a > b$, the new ratio is $(a-x)/(b-x)$, and

$$\frac{a-x}{b-x} > \frac{a}{b} \iff b(a-x) > a(b-x) \iff ab - bx > ab - ax \iff a > b$$

so the ratio rises whenever the transaction removes equal amounts from both and the ratio was above one. The size of the payment does not matter, and neither does the fact that it is a payment: any transaction that reduces current assets and current liabilities by the same amount has this effect. The same algebra run in reverse shows that adding equal amounts to both *lowers* a ratio above one, which is what part (e) does.

**(e)** Buying $\pounds 30{,}000$ of inventory on credit raises inventory to $\pounds 75{,}000$ and current liabilities to $\pounds 80{,}000$, so current assets become $\pounds 140{,}000$ (M1).

$$\text{current ratio} = \frac{140{,}000}{80{,}000} = 1.75 \tag{A1}$$

The acid test numerator is unchanged, because the $\pounds 30{,}000$ added to inventory is subtracted again (M1):

$$\frac{140{,}000 - 75{,}000}{80{,}000} = \frac{65{,}000}{80{,}000} = 0.8125 \approx 0.81 \tag{A1}$$

The two transactions together have moved the current ratio from 2.00 to 1.75 and the acid test from 1.25 to 0.81, so on balance the liquidity position is weaker, not stronger (A1).

The acid test is the ratio that should be read here, and the current ratio is the one that flatters. At 1.75 the current ratio still looks comfortable, and it has fallen by less than the acid test because inventory is doing the work: inventory is now $\pounds 75{,}000$ of $\pounds 140{,}000$ of current assets, so more than half of what the business counts as liquid is stock that has to be sold before it becomes cash. The acid test has crossed below 1.00, which means the business cannot settle its current liabilities from the assets it already holds in near-cash form. It would have to sell inventory, and selling inventory is what generates the receivables and cash in the first place, so the position is circular rather than merely tight.

The evaluation is not one-sided, however. The $\pounds 30{,}000$ of inventory was bought to be sold, and if it turns over as the existing stock does it will convert into receivables and then cash within the working capital cycle, restoring the acid test without any new financing. The $\pounds 10{,}000$ paid to the supplier also released credit and may have earned a settlement discount. So the transactions weaken the *reported* liquidity position while leaving the *underlying* trading position intact, and the honest conclusion is that the ratios have moved in a way the business should monitor rather than a way that shows it is in difficulty. What the figures cannot settle is how quickly the new inventory will turn over, and that is the question a lender would ask next.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) One mark each for 37.5%, 12.5% and 8.0%, with the working shown for at least one. Award the marks for the three percentages even if the candidate does not comment on the pattern; the comment is offered in the answer and is not required.

(b) One mark for capital employed of 300,000, one for the ROCE of 20.0%, and one for using operating profit rather than net profit in the numerator. A candidate who uses net profit and obtains 12.8% should be awarded the first mark only, and the same applies to a candidate who uses equity alone and obtains 30.0%, because in both cases the denominator or the numerator has been chosen wrongly rather than miscalculated.

(c) One mark for current assets of 120,000, one for 2.00, one for 1.25 with inventory removed from the numerator. A candidate who divides inventory by current liabilities, or who includes inventory in the acid test, scores the first mark only.

(d) One mark for the revised figures, one for both ratios and the direction of change, one for the explanation that equal amounts leave the top and bottom of a fraction above one. The explanation mark requires the condition that the ratio exceeds one; a candidate who says "paying a debt always improves liquidity" has stated a rule that is false for a ratio below one and earns no marks for the explanation.

(e) One mark for the revised current assets and liabilities, one for 1.75, one for the observation that the acid test numerator is unchanged, one for 0.81. The evaluation mark is awarded for a conclusion that distinguishes the reported ratio movement from the underlying trading position; a bare "liquidity is worse because the acid test fell" scores 0 for the evaluation, because it does not engage with the fact that the inventory was bought to be sold.

Forfeits: treating the acid test numerator as unchanged in part (d), which happens if the candidate applies the cancellation rule to the wrong transaction and obtains 1.25 again; reporting the acid test as 0.83 by adding the inventory to current assets without adjusting the denominator. Condonation: a candidate who writes the ratios as fractions rather than decimals, or who rounds 0.8125 to 0.81 or 0.813, should be given full credit.
questions.explanation:
Ratio analysis is taught as a set of formulas and marked as a set of answers, and the formulas are reliable enough that a student can score well on them without ever forming an opinion about what a ratio is. This item is aimed at the gap between using a ratio and reasoning with one. Parts (a) to (c) are the routine application, and they are included so that the item has a floor: a student who can do the arithmetic has something to show for the work. Parts (d) and (e) ask a different kind of question, and they cannot be answered by substituting into a formula at all.

The transaction in part (d) is counter-intuitive in a way that catches almost everyone the first time. A business pays its debts and its liquidity ratios improve; a business that pays its debts is poorer in cash and its ratios improve. Both statements are true, and the reason is that a ratio is a comparison rather than a measurement, so changing the numbers on both sides of it changes the comparison itself. The condition that decides the direction is whether the ratio was above one, and it is a property of the ratio and not of the transaction. Once a student has seen the algebra, the result stops being paradoxical, and the size of the payment stops mattering at all -- a theme the item makes explicit, because the instinct is to explain the movement by saying that ten thousand pounds is small.

Part (e) then turns the same machinery through ninety degrees. Buying inventory on credit adds equal amounts to current assets and current liabilities, so the equal-amounts rule applies and the current ratio falls. The acid test is the interesting case, because it subtracts inventory from the numerator, and the addition and the subtraction cancel exactly: the numerator is untouched while the denominator rises, so the ratio must fall and it falls below one. A student who has only memorised the equal-amounts rule will get the current ratio right and the acid test wrong, and the two answers will disagree with each other in a way that is visible on the page.

The final evaluation is deliberately open. The ratios have weakened and the conclusion that the position is weaker is defensible; so is the conclusion that the position is unchanged, because the inventory was bought to be sold and the acid test will recover as it turns over. What the item will not accept is a conclusion that ignores the reason the inventory is there. This is the standard AO3 demand in Business Management -- use the figures to reach a judgement, and recognise the limit of what the figures can show -- and it is the part of the subject that a purely computational preparation leaves out.

provenance.inspired_by: A-Level Business ratio-analysis questions that ask for the effect of a transaction on the current ratio and the acid test ratio
provenance.adaptation: The archetype is the "state and explain the effect of a transaction on the liquidity ratios" question found in A-Level Business, combined with a full ratio extract. The figures, the two-transaction sequence, the cancellation in the acid test and the evaluation part are written here.
provenance.resource_origin: A-Level Business studies material on profitability and liquidity ratio analysis, including exercises on the effect of transactions on the current and acid test ratios

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Compute the two ratios before and after each transaction, notice that the current assets and the current liabilities each change by the same amount, and conclude that the acid test must move in the same direction and by a similar amount as the current ratio, because both fractions have had the same amount added to the top and to the bottom.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The acid test subtracts inventory from current assets, so buying inventory on credit adds thirty thousand pounds to the numerator and then removes it again in the same subtraction, leaving the numerator at sixty five thousand while the denominator rises to eighty thousand, and the ratio falls through one while the current ratio merely falls from two point two to one point seven five.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: The acid test is reported as rising along with the current ratio, or as unchanged at 1.30, because the cancellation inside the numerator is not noticed, and the liquidity position is judged to be comfortable on a current ratio of 1.75 when the near-cash cover has in fact dropped below one.

verification.method: Every ratio was recomputed from the balances rather than carried across: the income statement was rebuilt from revenue downwards, the current assets and current liabilities were re-derived after each transaction, and the acid test was computed both directly and as current assets minus inventory over current liabilities. The direction of change was confirmed algebraically as well as numerically, by checking that (a-x)/(b-x) exceeds a/b if and only if a exceeds b for the values used.
solution_skeleton: rebuild the income statement down to net profit
compute capital employed and the return on it
compute both liquidity ratios at the opening position
re-derive the ratios after the cash payment and show both rise
show the acid test numerator is unchanged by the credit purchase

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.syllabus_ref: 5.5 Break-even analysis (contribution, break-even output, margin of safety, target profit); 3.3 Costs and revenues
questions.subtopic: 5.5 A break-even output above the capacity ceiling: a negative margin of safety and the three single levers that would close the gap
questions.challenge_mechanism: Break-even analysis answers the question "how many units must we sell", and the answer is treated as achievable because the formula does not contain a capacity. Here the answer is 12 500 units and the kiln line can produce 10 000, so the arithmetic is correct and the conclusion it invites -- that the business becomes profitable above 12 500 units -- describes a region the business cannot enter. Contribution per unit is positive, so the loss shrinks as output rises, which means the best available outcome is the worst-looking one: full capacity is the least unprofitable point, and the margin of safety is negative rather than small.
questions.question: Ridgeway Ceramics makes a single product on one kiln line. The selling price is $\pounds 40$ per unit and the variable cost is $\pounds 24$ per unit. Annual fixed costs are $\pounds 200{,}000$. The kiln line can produce at most $10{,}000$ units in a year, and there is no way to add a second line within the year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the contribution per unit and the break-even output.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the margin of safety in units and as a percentage of capacity, and explain what a negative margin of safety means for this business.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that the best result Ridgeway Ceramics can achieve in a year is a loss of $\pounds 40{,}000$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the value of the selling price at which the business would exactly break even at its current capacity, and state the corresponding value for the annual fixed costs and for the variable cost per unit, taking each of the three on its own.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Evaluate which of the three changes in part (d) the management of Ridgeway Ceramics is most likely to be able to make, and justify your answer.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Contribution per unit is the selling price less the variable cost per unit (M1):

$$\pounds 40 - \pounds 24 = \pounds 16 \tag{A1}$$

Break-even output is fixed costs divided by contribution per unit (A1):

$$\frac{200{,}000}{16} = 12{,}500 \text{ units}$$

**(b)** The margin of safety is the amount by which the planned output exceeds the break-even output, so with output at the capacity ceiling (M1):

$$10{,}000 - 12{,}500 = -2{,}500 \text{ units}$$

As a percentage of capacity (A1):

$$\frac{-2{,}500}{10{,}000} \times 100 = -25\%$$

A negative margin of safety means the business cannot reach break-even at any output it is able to produce (A1). Every unit it makes sells for $\pounds 16$ more than its variable cost, and that contribution is never enough to cover $\pounds 200{,}000$ of fixed costs, so the business makes a loss in every year in which it operates. The negative figure is not a shortfall to be made up by selling harder; it is a statement that the break-even point lies outside the set of outputs the business can reach.

**(c)** At full capacity the total contribution is (M1)

$$10{,}000 \times \pounds 16 = \pounds 160{,}000$$

and the loss is the fixed costs less that contribution (A1):

$$\pounds 160{,}000 - \pounds 200{,}000 = -\pounds 40{,}000$$

Because contribution per unit is positive, each additional unit sold reduces the loss by $\pounds 16$, so profit increases with output throughout the feasible range (M1). The largest output the line can produce is therefore the least unprofitable one, and $\pounds 40{,}000$ is a loss at the best point rather than at a poor one: there is no output at which Ridgeway Ceramics makes a profit, so the maximum profit it can achieve in a year is a loss of $\pounds 40{,}000$.

**(d)** Each change is found by setting the total contribution at capacity equal to the fixed costs.

For the selling price, let it be $p$ (M1):

$$10{,}000(p - 24) = 200{,}000 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p - 24 = 20 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p = \pounds 44.00 \tag{A1}$$

For the annual fixed costs, with contribution per unit still $\pounds 16$:

$$10{,}000 \times 16 = \pounds 160{,}000 \tag{A1}$$

For the variable cost per unit, let it be $v$:

$$10{,}000(40 - v) = 200{,}000 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 40 - v = 20 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v = \pounds 20.00 \tag{A1}$$

So the three thresholds are a price of $\pounds 44.00$ (a rise of $\pounds 4.00$, or 10%), fixed costs of $\pounds 160{,}000$ (a cut of $\pounds 40{,}000$, or 20%) and a variable cost of $\pounds 20.00$ (a cut of $\pounds 4.00$, or 16.7%). Each figure is a threshold and not a target: at exactly that value the business breaks even at full capacity and makes nothing, so any of the three has to be bettered before a profit appears.

**(e)** The three changes are not equally available, and the comparison has to be made on two axes: how large the change is, and whether the business controls it.

The price rise is the smallest proportional change and it requires no investment, no renegotiation and no new equipment, which makes it attractive on paper. It is also the least likely to hold. Ridgeway sells a single product into a market it does not control, and a 10% rise has to be accepted by every customer for the arithmetic to work; if it is accepted by fewer, the contribution gain on the remaining units does not compensate for the volume lost, and at a price of $\pounds 44$ the business needs *all* 10 000 units to break even, leaving no room for any loss of demand at all. The remedy that looks cleanest is the one with the narrowest margin for error.

The fixed-cost cut is the largest change in absolute terms, $\pounds 40{,}000$, and it is the one the business controls most directly, since fixed costs are largely internal commitments. But the kiln line is the fixed cost that matters, and it cannot be halved; a 20% reduction in a single-line ceramics business means cutting maintenance, staffing or the second shift, and cutting the second shift is precisely what would reduce capacity and make the position worse. A fixed-cost cut that lowers the ceiling lowers the output the business can sell, and the break-even output would have to be recalculated against the smaller capacity rather than assumed unchanged.

The variable-cost cut is the one most likely to be achievable. $\pounds 4.00$ per unit is a 16.7% reduction in the cost of materials and power, and variable costs are the category a manufacturer can most often attack: renegotiating a clay or glaze contract, reducing kiln waste, buying in larger quantities. It requires no change to the price the customer sees and no reduction in capacity, so it does not trade one problem for another. The difficulty is that a 16.7% cut is substantial for a business whose inputs are commodity-like, and any saving is likely to arrive in stages rather than at once.

Taken together, the most likely single change is the variable-cost reduction, and the strongest reason is not that it is the largest or the smallest but that it is the only one that leaves the capacity ceiling and the selling price untouched. The most reliable answer, however, is not to rely on any single lever: a smaller price rise combined with a smaller variable-cost reduction reaches the same threshold while exposing the business to less risk on either one, and a management that pursues only one of the three is betting the whole recovery on the assumption that is hardest to verify. What the figures cannot show is how the market would respond to a price rise or how far a supplier would move, and those are the questions that decide between the options.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) One mark for the contribution of 16, one for dividing fixed costs by contribution, one for 12 500 units. A candidate who computes 200 000/24 scores no marks, because 24 is the variable cost rather than the contribution.

(b) One mark for subtracting the break-even output from capacity, one for -25%, one for the meaning. The meaning mark requires the candidate to say that break-even is unreachable at any feasible output; "the margin of safety is low" does not earn it, because the sign is the point.

(c) One mark for the total contribution at capacity, one for the loss of 40 000, one for the observation that positive contribution per unit makes the largest output the least unprofitable. A candidate who computes the loss at some other output, or who reports a profit, cannot score the third mark.

(d) One mark for setting total contribution equal to fixed costs in the price case, and one mark for each of the three thresholds: 44.00, 160 000 and 20.00. Follow-through applies: a candidate who used the wrong contribution in (a) but applies a consistent method should be given the method marks.

(e) The evaluation mark is awarded for a judgement that names one change as most likely and supports it with a reason that distinguishes the three. The remaining marks are for engaging with at least two of the three in terms of feasibility rather than arithmetic -- for example that the price rise has the least margin for error because it needs full volume, or that a fixed-cost cut may reduce capacity. A response that lists the three percentage changes without judging between them scores 0 for the evaluation.

Forfeits: computing the margin of safety as 12 500 - 10 000 = 2 500 and reporting it as positive, which reverses the entire item; treating 12 500 units as achievable and reporting a profit at that output. Condonation: a candidate who expresses the fixed-cost threshold as a 20% reduction rather than as 160 000, and who shows the working, should be given full credit.
questions.explanation:
Break-even is the first quantitative tool a business student meets, and it is almost always presented as a question with an answer: how many units must we sell? The formula is short, the answer is a number, and the number is treated as reachable. This item is built on the observation that the formula contains no capacity, so it will happily produce an answer the business cannot act on. Nothing in the calculation is wrong; what is wrong is the assumption, imported from every exercise the student has seen, that the break-even output is within the range of outputs the business can produce.

That assumption is normally harmless, which is what makes it worth attacking. In a well-posed question the break-even point sits below capacity, the margin of safety is positive, and the tool behaves as advertised. Here it sits 2 500 units above capacity, and every conclusion drawn from the standard reading of the result inverts: the business cannot become profitable by selling more, because selling more is already the best it can do and it still loses money. The margin of safety, which students are taught to read as a cushion, becomes a measure of how far outside the achievable range the break-even point lies.

The item also rewards a student who understands what contribution per unit does and does not mean. A positive contribution means each unit reduces the loss, so the loss is smallest at the largest feasible output. A student who has memorised "profit rises with output above break-even" will look for the profitable region and find none, and the honest conclusion -- that the best available outcome is a loss -- is the one the item is testing for. That conclusion is uncomfortable, and reaching it requires the student to report a result that no textbook exercise would ask for.

The final part moves the item from analysis to judgement, which is where the Business Management assessment objectives live. Three thresholds have been calculated and they are arithmetically interchangeable; deciding between them requires knowledge of the business that the numbers do not contain. The item does not have a single right answer, and it is marked as though it does not: what is assessed is whether the student can say why one lever is more available than another, and whether they notice that a fixed-cost cut in a single-line manufacturer may take capacity down with it. That last observation is the one that separates a student who has understood the model from one who has only learned to use it.

provenance.inspired_by: A-Level Business break-even questions that extend the standard calculation to a capacity limit and a set of possible remedies
provenance.adaptation: The archetype is the standard break-even exercise with contribution and margin of safety. The single-line capacity ceiling, the three-lever threshold analysis and the evaluation part are written here.
provenance.resource_origin: A-Level Business studies material on break-even analysis, contribution and margin of safety, extended here to a capacity constraint

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Apply the break-even formula, obtain 12 500 units, and treat that figure as the output the business must reach, then read the margin of safety as a shortfall to be closed by selling more and report that the business becomes profitable once it passes 12 500 units.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The kiln line cannot produce more than 10 000 units, so the break-even output lies outside the set of outputs the business can reach and there is no profitable region at all; because contribution per unit is positive the loss is smallest at the largest feasible output, which makes the best achievable result a loss of 40 000 rather than a profit at 12 500 units.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: The business is reported as breaking even at 12 500 units and as making a profit above it, and the margin of safety is reported as 2 500 units or as a 25% shortfall that further sales would close, when in fact every output the business can produce loses money and the only lever is to change one of the three variables that set the break-even point.

verification.method: Every figure was recomputed from first principles rather than from the formula alone: the profit at capacity was rebuilt as total revenue less variable and fixed costs and checked against total contribution less fixed costs, the three thresholds were each substituted back to confirm that profit is exactly zero at that value, and the margin of safety was checked to be negative before it was reported as such.
solution_skeleton: compute contribution and the break-even output
compare the break-even output with the capacity ceiling
show the loss at capacity is the best available result
solve each variable for a zero profit at capacity
weigh the three thresholds by feasibility rather than size
